## TL;DR

I exercised the web app (Work board, task drawer, Agents, Settings) under three
failure modes — dead server, HTTP 500s, and responses that stall past the
client's own timeouts — using headless WebKit with Playwright request
interception only, at 375/768/1280 px. Three real defects came out of it and are
fixed: a stalled `/api/auth/me` froze the entire app behind an endless
skeleton; the offline banner outlived a page that had already recovered on its
own; and Settings showed an endless skeleton when `/api/config` failed. Each
fix has unit tests, and the whole pass is captured in a new 9-test headless
browser suite plus `docs/qa/2026-11-offline-slow-network-qa.md`.

## Work and rationale

**Method.** The QA criterion bans visible browsers and real outages, so every
failure mode is produced with `page.route` interception against the built app
served from a throwaway fixture root (the shared `ui-harness.ts` WebKit
launch). I extended the harness's structural route type with what interception
actually needs: `abort` (offline), `fetch` + `fulfill({ response })`
(slow-then-real passthrough), and `unroute` (recovery). Keeping these
structural — not importing Playwright types directly — is consistent with the
existing smoke harness pattern, and the real `Route` object satisfies the
interface unchanged.

**Fix 1 — the stalled auth check was the highest-severity finding.** The auth
store's `/api/auth/me` call is plain `fetch` with no timeout, and both the
router guard and `App.vue`'s `onMounted` await it before anything renders. A
server that accepts the connection but never answers — the "slow" case, which
is exactly what a half-loaded laptop under memory pressure looks like — left
every page spinning forever with no message. I bounded the request at 6 s with
an `AbortController`; a timeout is treated like any other auth failure (auth
off, app renders normally), and a reload picks up the real answer. I chose 6 s
because the auth check gates first paint: generous enough for a genuinely slow
server, short enough that the skeleton never reads as "stuck" to a human.

**Fix 2 — the banner contradicted the page.** The Work board already recovers
on its own: the SSE stream reconnects with jittered backoff and every
reconnect triggers a full board refresh. But the "…is not running" banner
stayed up until the user focused or navigated, because `checkUiBuild` only
re-probes on focus/navigation. A page that visibly fills in with data while
still claiming the server is offline is worse than either state alone. The fix
is `clearOfflineOnStreamBack()`: the moment the stream is demonstrably back,
the offline banner clears — never while a manual reload is in flight, and
never for a stale-build banner (those have different truth conditions and must
not be silently dismissed by a stream reconnect).

**Fix 3 — Settings' endless skeleton.** When `/api/config` failed, the tab
strip rendered (it's real chrome) but the panel body waited on a config that
would never arrive. Settings now shows "Couldn't load settings" with a Retry
button, and the skeleton is suppressed once failure is known (otherwise the
error panel and skeleton would both render). The panel reuses the styling
Agents already had, generalized from `.agents-load-error` to a shared
`.page-load-error` class, so both surfaces present the same recoverable
pattern.

**Regression tests.** `offline-slow-network-browser.test.ts` drives the whole
matrix: offline and 500 across the four surfaces, the stalled-auth boot, the
stalled health/board banner, self-recovery with banner clearing, and a
`scrollWidth − innerWidth` overflow check per panel at all three widths. It
skips cleanly without Playwright, like the other browser gates. Unit tests
cover the three fixes directly (`auth-stall.test.ts`, `ui-recovery.test.ts`,
`settings-load-error.test.ts`). For review visibility I added two capture-only
shot fixtures, `settings:loadFailed` and `agents:loadFailed`, which pin the
config store into the failed-load state the panels react to — the declared
shots can show the error panels without an unhealthy preview.

**Deliberately not claimed.** The Hub loads this same SPA in its WebView, so
every page-level behavior applies to it, but the native (Capacitor) shell's own
loading/return-to-picker screens were not driven — that needs a real device and
is out of scope for an interception-only pass. The doc says so explicitly
rather than implying the Hub was fully covered.

## Approaches tried

- For the recovery test I first tried asserting the banner clears on focus
  (the existing re-probe path), but that tests the old behavior. Intercepting
  the API, letting the SSE reconnect fire, and asserting the banner drops with
  no user action is the honest test of the fix.
- For "slow" I initially faked delayed responses with `fulfill` after a
  `setTimeout`, but the more valuable scenario is "stalls past the client's own
  timeout" — that's what produces a *reported* failure instead of a hang, and
  it's how the stalled-auth bug was found. The suite covers both: stalled
  `/api/auth/me`, and stalled `/api/health` + `/api/board`.
- I considered handling the auth stall with a global fetch wrapper, but the
  timeout belongs at the one call site that gates boot; a wrapper would widen
  behavior for every fetch call without a test per consumer.

## Challenges and blockers

This session resumed after earlier engineer runs exited with errors, so the
worktree already held the implementation in WIP checkpoint commits. My first
test run failed confusingly (62 failures, "install @vitejs/plugin-vue to
handle .vue files"): I had run vitest directly, bypassing the repo's two-pass
`bun run test` wrapper and its config. With the proper runner the same suites
pass — a reminder that "the tests are broken" here usually means "I invoked
them wrong", exactly what AGENTS.md warns about. No unresolved blockers; no
human-only step was needed for anything I claimed.

One blocker appeared at check time and turned out to be environmental: the
first remote-validation run of the rendered contrast audit reported 154
`clear-light` settings failures — every settings row showing light-theme text
over the *dark* theme's panel color, i.e. a mixed-theme sample — and it
survived the audit's own phantom-failure retry, which made it look like a real
regression. Since the diff touches no theme token and the flagged screen
renders identically on `main`, I chased it on the runner itself: the gate runs
inside the `repoos-ci` container, and re-running the identical commit there
minutes later passed the audit twice in one run with zero findings. The
#0596/#0617 history documents this exact class. I recorded it as a
load-dependent audit flake in the QA doc rather than "fixing" anything — the
honest disposition was evidence, not a defensive CSS change.

## Key learnings

- A QA pass over *failure modes* is most valuable when it hunts for "hangs
  silently", not "shows the wrong message": all three real bugs were variants
  of an unbounded wait, while every surface already had decent error copy.
- Await-chains through router guards and `onMounted` turn any single
  unbounded request into a whole-app freeze — timeout budgets belong on
  boot-critical calls first.
- A recovery banner is a claim about the world; it must be retracted the
  moment that claim is false, not when the user next interacts.
- Reusing one error-panel pattern (`.page-load-error`) across surfaces keeps
  the plain-English behavior testable once and present everywhere.
